cards.front: How many letters does tajwīd count in the Arabic alphabet?
cards.back: 29 — the common count of 28 treats the hamzah and the alif as one letter; tajwīd counts them apart.

cards.front: On what basis did the scholars arrange the Arabic letters in their alphabetical order?
cards.back: By similarity of written shape, so letters that look alike sit together: <bdi>ب ت ث</bdi>, <bdi>ج ح خ</bdi>, <bdi>د ذ</bdi>.

cards.front: How did the scholars tell apart letters that share one written shape, such as <bdi>ب ت ث</bdi>?
cards.back: They added dots (iʿjām). The step is credited to Naṣr ibn ʿĀṣim and Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmar, in the 1st century AH.

cards.front: The first letter of the alphabet is written as an alif. Which letter is it really?
cards.back: The hamzah. The true alif is the madd alif, which can never begin a word; old alphabet lists show it inside <bdi>لا</bdi> (lām-alif).

cards.front: What vowel is on the letter before a madd alif?
cards.back: Always a fatḥah. The alif itself is always sākin; it never occurs any other way.

cards.text: Your notes divide the mouth (al-fam) into the {{c1::upper palate}}, the {{c2::tongue}}, the {{c3::teeth}} and the {{c4::lips}}.

cards.meaning: the top of the throat (the part nearest the mouth), level with the root of the tongue
the middle of the throat, at the epiglottis
the bottom of the throat (the part farthest from the mouth), at the vocal cords
the gums: the ridge just behind the upper front teeth
the pre-palate: the front of the palate, just behind the gums
the hard palate
the soft palate, behind the hard palate
the uvula
the root of the tongue, facing the throat
the back of the tongue (its furthest part), below the soft palate
the middle of the tongue, below the hard palate
the blade of the tongue: just behind the very tip
the very tip of the tongue

cards.front: Which tongue term sounds as if it means the tip, but names the part just behind it?
cards.back: Ṭaraf al-lisān (the blade). The very tip is raʾs al-lisān.

cards.meaning: the side edge of the tongue, on both sides
the back of the side edge, up to (not including) the root
the front-middle of the side edge, level with the blade (ṭaraf)
the front end of the side edge, level with the tip (raʾs)

cards.front: What is sound, physically?
cards.back: A vibration of air molecules that the human ear can perceive.

cards.front: Between what frequencies can the human ear perceive sound?
cards.back: About 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz (20 kHz). The top of the range falls with age.

cards.text: Sound arises in four ways: {{c1::collision}} of two objects (a clap); {{c2::separation}} of two objects held together by cohesion (snapping a twig); {{c3::vibration}} of an object (a plucked string); {{c4::friction}} of one object against another (rubbing hands).

cards.front: How is a letter (ḥarf) defined in tajwīd?
cards.back: A sound that relies on an articulation point, either specific (muḥaqqaq) or approximate (muqaddar).

cards.front: In the definition of a letter, what makes an articulation point approximate (muqaddar) rather than specific?
cards.back: The sound hits no particular organ. This is true of the madd letters, which come from the jawf.

cards.front: What physically produces a sākin letter?
cards.back: A collision (qarʿ) between two parts of the speech organs, as when the lips press together on a sākin bāʾ.

cards.front: What physically produces a letter that carries a vowel (mutaḥarrik)?
cards.back: Two parts of the speech organs separating (qalʿ), together with the articulation of the vowel's own source: a fatḥah comes from the alif's, a ḍammah from the wāw's, a kasrah from the yāʾ's.

cards.front: What physically produces the madd and līn letters?
cards.back: Vibration of the vocal cords, shaped by a mouth position particular to each letter; no two organs meet.

cards.front: Which letters originate in al-jawf?
cards.back: The madd letters: alif, wāw and yāʾ when they lengthen the vowel before them.

cards.front: When is a wāw a madd letter?
cards.back: When it is sākin and the letter before it has a ḍammah, as in <bdi>يَقُولُ</bdi>.

cards.front: When is a yāʾ a madd letter?
cards.back: When it is sākin and the letter before it has a kasrah, as in <bdi>قِيلَ</bdi>.

cards.front: How long is a madd letter held when nothing after it calls for more?
cards.back: 2 counts — the natural madd (madd ṭabīʿī).

cards.front: How must the lengths of the fatḥah, kasrah and ḍammah compare?
cards.back: They must all be equal: every short vowel gets the same single count.

cards.front: What is the recitation mistake called ikhtilās?
cards.back: Shortening a vowel: taking away part of its sound, so it comes out shorter than the others. It is a mistake except where a reading calls for it, as in one of Ḥafṣ's two ways of reading <bdi>تَأْمَنَّا</bdi> (Yūsuf 12:11).

cards.front: What is it called when the lips push forward on a heavy letter?
cards.back: Ishmām. Heaviness comes from the back of the tongue rising, never from the lips. Ishmām is a mistake except where a reading calls for it: in Ḥafṣ, in <bdi>تَأْمَنَّا</bdi> (Yūsuf 12:11), and as an option when stopping on a ḍammah.

cards.front: Where must the tongue be for a madd alif?
cards.back: Down, so the sound passes from the jawf through the throat and mouth unobstructed.

cards.front: What must the jaw do for a madd alif?
cards.back: Open: the space between the upper and lower back teeth must be open.

cards.front: What happens to a madd alif if the tongue isn't down or the jaw isn't open?
cards.back: It takes on a kasrah sound: taqlīl (a slight lean toward yāʾ) or imālah (a full lean). Both are mistakes in Ḥafṣ, except the one imālah in <bdi>مجراها</bdi> (Hūd 11:41).

cards.front: Where does the tongue go for a madd wāw?
cards.back: A little back, but the sound's path stays unobstructed.

cards.front: What shape do the lips take for a madd wāw?
cards.back: Rounded, like an O. (On heavy letters, by contrast, the lips must not move forward.)

cards.front: What does the tongue do for a madd yāʾ?
cards.back: Its middle rises up and back while the front goes down, still leaving room for the sound.

cards.front: In a madd yāʾ the middle of the tongue rises. What keeps room for the sound?
cards.back: The lower jaw drops a little more.

cards.front: How does the sound of all three madd letters travel from the vocal cords to the outside?
cards.back: Without spreading: it goes out as a straight, focused stream.

cards.meaning: the upper palate
the tongue
the teeth
the lips
adding dots to letters that share a written shape
specific (of an articulation point): the sound hits a particular organ
approximate (of an articulation point): the sound hits no particular organ
collision of two parts of the speech organs
separation of two parts of the speech organs
wāw or yāʾ sākinah after a fatḥah, as in <bdi>خَوْف</bdi> and <bdi>بَيْت</bdi>
the natural madd: a madd letter held for 2 counts
a slight lean, halfway between a plain fatḥah and imālah
a full lean: the fatḥah toward a kasrah, and the alif after it toward a yāʾ
